<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS6" title="In 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.6 </span>Effect of Prefix Length on Discovering PA Memorization</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS7" title="In 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.7 </span>Qualitative Analysis</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS8" title="In 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.8 </span>Limitations</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S5" title="In Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5 </span>Related Work</span></a></li>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>

</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training data leakage from Large Language Models (LLMs) has been a concern for many reasons. Two important concerns include a) copyright and licensing violations, which have been the subject of several lawsuits and prior literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karamolegkou et al. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tremblay v. OpenAI, Inc. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">The New York Times Company v. Microsoft Corporation (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chang et al. (2023)</a></cite>, and b) leakage of sensitive data, such as Personally Identifiable Information (PII) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mozes et al. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2021)</a></cite>. Starting with  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2021)</a></cite>, several studies have attempted to quantify LLM training data leakage, often using various metrics to
benchmark the extraction of training data in different training and inference scenarios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karamolegkou et al. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al. (2024)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prior approaches to quantifying memorization in LLMs often overlook the models’ capacity to generalize, conflating genuine memorization with the generation of statistically common sequences <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite>. For example, a prompt like “The murder was committed by” may yield “John Doe” with high probability not because the model memorized this sequence from training, but because “John Doe” is a common placeholder name. Recent work confirms that LLMs can reproduce text verbatim by generalizing from related patterns rather than recalling specific examples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite>. Thus, statistically likely sequences should not be classified as memorized.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A current, robust approach to account for such generalization is <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Counterfactual Memorization</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Counterfactual memorization is traditionally measured by computing the difference between the likelihood of leaking a training sequence from a model that was trained with versus without a given sequence. If a given sequence has a high probability of leakage in both models, then it is probably not counterfactually memorized. Naturally, an explicit computation of this difference may be very expensive, as it requires us to train several “counterfactual” or “baseline” models for every training sequence. These measurements also often necessitate tightly controlled settings, making them very impractical to reproduce on production language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a></cite>. As a result, prior studies on counterfactual memorization have been limited in scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghosh et al. (2025)</a></cite>. This motivates the need for a cheaper method for filtering out “popular” sequences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address this limitation, we introduce a new criterion for filtering out statistically likely outputs (suffixes) by assessing whether they are strongly associated <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only</em> with their specific training prompts (prefixes). We term this phenomenon <em id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Prior-Aware memorization</em> (PA memorization). This framework distinguishes genuine memorization from statistical likelihood by testing whether a sequence retains high generation probability even when the model is prompted with randomly sampled text from the training data. If a suffix appears with high confidence across many unrelated prefixes, its likelihood arises from generalization—reflecting statistical commonality—rather than from memorization of a specific prefix–suffix pair.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A key advantage of PA memorization is that it requires no additional model training, making it substantially more computationally efficient than counterfactual memorization. Furthermore, to provide evidence that PA memorization effectively filters out statistically likely sequences, we present an empirical comparison with Counterfactual Memorization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our methodology on text from the training corpus of two pre-trained models: Llama, and OPT. Our target sequences were either a) randomly sampled long sequences (to simulate copyright-infringement scenarios), or b) Named Entities (<em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.,</em>names of individuals, places, etc.) to simulate the risk of leaking Personally Identifying Information (PII). We find that using the largest OPT and LLama models, <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="55-90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>55</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">55-90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the sequences that would earlier be labeled as memorized are in fact statistically common sequences. More surprisingly, we note that a similar result occurs even with the SATML training data extraction challenge dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, where around <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\%</annotation></semantics></math> of sequences are “common” in nature.
This is despite the fact that each sequence in the challenge dataset occurs only once in the entire training data. Our findings highlight the significance of looking beyond the low-frequency of exact copies in the training data when labeling a sequence as memorized, and urge us to rethink some of our previous notions about memorization in LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of this work is organized as follows: in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Generalization vs Memorization: Issues with leakage measures ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we outline the current research gaps to motivate the need for our work. Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> includes the definitions of the metrics we use for our experimental results. We present our findings in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and highlight any novel conclusions. Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Related Work ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> outlines related literature, and we conclude this work in Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Conclusion ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Generalization vs Memorization: Issues with leakage measures</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Most prior work considers training data that can be produced verbatim with high probability to be “memorized” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2021)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al. (2024)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite>. However, as noted above, such methods may misclassify popular sequences as memorized. To make this limitation precise, consider a prefix <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and suffix <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s\in D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s\in D</annotation></semantics></math> indicating that their concatenation occurs in the dataset <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>. Existing metrics typically label such a sequence as memorized if the conditional probability <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> is large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, which we refer henceforth to <em id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">extractable memorization</em>. Extrctable memorization is reasonable: under maximum likelihood training, the model’s objective is to maximize <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\prod_{(p,s)\in D}P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∏</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\prod_{(p,s)\in D}P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math>, so if a model has genuinely memorized a given <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="S2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> should indeed be high.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, the converse is not necessarily true—i.e., a high conditional probability does not necessarily imply memorization. This is because <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> can be high for two distinct reasons, which we formally decompose using Bayes’ rule:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)=\frac{P(p\mid s)\cdot P(s)}{P(p)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>s</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)=\frac{P(p\mid s)\cdot P(s)}{P(p)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Indeed, <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> can be high if:</p>
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> is very large, suggesting that <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> may be statistically popular (generic). For instance, in the sequence if <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> = “The murder was committed by” and <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> = “John Doe”, <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> may be large because <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is a popular occurrence in the dataset.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If the relative belief ratio <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(p\mid s)}{P(p)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(p\mid s)}{P(p)}</annotation></semantics></math> is large. This would happen if <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(p)</annotation></semantics></math> is small (<em id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.,</em>the prefix is a rare prefix in the dataset) relative to <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(p\mid s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(p\mid s)</annotation></semantics></math>, suggesting that the suffix is a strong indicator of the prefix, as we would expect for memorization.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">There have been alternative definitions of memorization, such that of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild et al. (2024)</a></cite>, which classifies a sequence as memorized if it can be generated with a compressed prompt. Similarly, concurrent work by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Morris et al. (2025)</a></cite> also defines a compression-based memorization metric using Kolmogorov complexity (which is not computable in general). However, it is unclear whether these alternative approaches can distinguish sequences <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> with statistically popular targets <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> from their truly memorized counterparts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, a stronger definition of memorization has been proposed, called <em id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Counterfactual Memorization</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a></cite>. This definition measures how models trained with and without the target sequence would perform on the sequence. A counterfactually memorized sequence is then categorized as a sequence that would not perform well on a model that was not explicitly trained on said sequence. If a sequence performs well on both models, it is said to be <em id="S2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generalizable</em>, since it can be produced by a model that was not trained on the sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Failing to account for generalization capabilities may greatly overestimate memorization, as indicated by a recent study <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite>. However, accurately computing Counterfactual Memorization can also be extremely expensive, as the model must be trained at least twice for every labeled sequence–once with the sequence, and, second, on the same training data absent the specific sequence. Naturally, for models with billions of parameters trained on many terabytes of text, this can quickly become infeasible. One may consider cheaper estimates to this calculation, such as training approximate baselines with a different data distribution; however, it is fundamentally difficult to make these estimates accurate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">All told, there is a clear need for an inexpensive, but accurate, method for identifying whether a particular training sequence is Counterfactually Memorized.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next propose and describe our approach to quantifying <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Prior-Aware</em> [ PA ] memorization, starting with a definition of this metric and proceeding to discuss how it can be feasibly computed. We empirically test our metric’s ability to filter out generic sequences by measuring its correlation Counterfactual Memorization from the literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Throughout this section, we presuppose a language model <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, defined as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmdefinition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmdefinition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmdefinition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmdefinition1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The language model <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> maps an input token sequence
<math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> to a distribution for the next token <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{j+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{j+1}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="M:p\mapsto P(\cdot\mid p)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M:p\mapsto P(\cdot\mid p).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We assume that the model <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is trained on a dataset <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>, consisting of sequences of prefix + suffix pairs <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> (where <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|</annotation></semantics></math> is the concatenation operator). We also assume that text generation proceeds auto-regressively from a starting sequence <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, and each time generating (and incorporating into <math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>) a subsequent token. We will use the notation <math id="S3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(x|y;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(x|y;M)</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the probability of generating sequence <math id="S3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> from such an application of <math id="S3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> to an initial sequence <math id="S3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(x;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(x;M)</annotation></semantics></math> will denote the total probability of seeing <math id="S3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> from any starting sequence.
Where the choice of model is clear, we may omit it for brevity, and write simply <math id="S3.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(x|y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(x|y)</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S3.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(x)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmdefinition2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmdefinition2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2</span></span><span id="Thmdefinition2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Prior-Aware memorization)<span id="Thmdefinition2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmdefinition2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmdefinition2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmdefinition2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For tunable thresholds <math id="Thmdefinition2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m,n\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m,n\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> we say that a sequence <math id="Thmdefinition2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s\in D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s\in D</annotation></semantics></math> is <em id="Thmdefinition2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">Prior-Aware memorized</em> by a model <math id="Thmdefinition2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="Thmdefinition2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p;M)&gt;m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p;M)&gt;m</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="Thmdefinition2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p;M)}{P(s;M)}&gt;n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p;M)}{P(s;M)}&gt;n</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Explanation.</span>
The definition imposes two requirements: First, that <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p;M)&gt;n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p;M)&gt;n</annotation></semantics></math> (see Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 𝑃(𝑠∣𝑝;𝑀): verbatim generation of 𝑠 given 𝑝 ‣ 3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), which ensures that the suffix <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> has a high probability of being generated verbatim by model <math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> when prompted with <math id="S3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. This has been adopted from prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a></cite>. Second, that the relative belief ratio, <math id="S3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tfrac{P(s\mid p;M)}{P(s;M)}&gt;m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tfrac{P(s\mid p;M)}{P(s;M)}&gt;m</annotation></semantics></math> (see Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 𝑃(𝑠,𝑀): generality of 𝑠 ‣ 3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>), implying that <math id="S3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is a strong indicator of <math id="S3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. A large ratio (<math id="S3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m&gt;&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&gt;&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m&gt;&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>) suggests that the presence of <math id="S3.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> predicts the presence of <math id="S3.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>, or, in other words, <math id="S3.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> was less likely to be generally produced by another sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To compute this metric for any given pair <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s\in D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s\in D</annotation></semantics></math>, we need to compute <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p;M)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s;M)</annotation></semantics></math>. We explain how to do this in the next two subsections.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span><math id="S3.SS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p;M)</annotation></semantics></math>: verbatim generation of <math id="S3.SS1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> given <math id="S3.SS1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For notational convenience, we write <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="t_{1:j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{1:j}</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the sequence of tokens
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math>. Using this notation, the probability of producing
a sequence of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="s=t_{j+1:j+k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=t_{j+1:j+k}</annotation></semantics></math> (suffix) when the model is
prompted with a <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>-token prefix <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p=t_{1:j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=t_{1:j}</annotation></semantics></math> is:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td colspan="2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\begin{split}P(s\mid p)=\prod_{i=j+1}^{j+k}P(t_{i}\mid t_{1:i-1})\end{split}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\begin{split}P(s\mid p)=\prod_{i=j+1}^{j+k}P(t_{i}\mid t_{1:i-1})\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 𝑃(𝑠∣𝑝;𝑀): verbatim generation of 𝑠 given 𝑝 ‣ 3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> is a closed form for the probability of leaking our target sequence verbatim from a given prefix. In practice, this metric can be computed from a single forward-pass per token, and we can thus
efficiently utilize this to compute whether <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)&gt;n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)&gt;n</annotation></semantics></math> for a given <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span><math id="S3.SS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s;M)</annotation></semantics></math>: generality of <math id="S3.SS2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The second component of our definition is <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}</annotation></semantics></math>. To compute the denominator, we would like to calculate the total probability over all prefixes <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> in the model’s vocabulary <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)~\hat{=}~v_{s}=\sum_{p_{i}\sim V^{*}}P(s\mid p_{i})\cdot P(p_{i})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.608em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mo>=</mo><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)~\hat{=}~v_{s}=\sum_{p_{i}\sim V^{*}}P(s\mid p_{i})\cdot P(p_{i})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, this calculation is computationally prohibitive. Instead, use an unbiased estimator <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> (inspired by Monte-Carlo Integration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Binder et al. (1992)</a></cite>) that converges to the true probability <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> as the number samples <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> grows to infinity.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmdefinition3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmdefinition3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3</span></span><span id="Thmdefinition3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmdefinition3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmdefinition3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmdefinition3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Given samples <math id="Thmdefinition3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{0},q_{1},\ldots q_{c-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{0},q_{1},\ldots q_{c-1}</annotation></semantics></math> chosen independently and identically according to the distribution of prefixes <math id="Thmdefinition3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}\sim V^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}\sim V^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, our <em id="Thmdefinition3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">total probability estimator</em> is given by</span></p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}_{s}=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=0}^{c}P(s\mid q_{i})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>c</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>c</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}_{s}=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=0}^{c}P(s\mid q_{i})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Note this estimator requires samples <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> to match the distribution of prefixes <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}\sim V^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}\sim V^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and it is thus computed for a specific model <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>; for brevity, we omit <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> from the notation where it can be straightforwardly inferred. The next two theorems show that <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> is unbiased.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E[\hat{v_{s}}]=v_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E[\hat{v_{s}}]=v_{s}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">By linearity of expectation, <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E[\hat{v_{s}}]=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{c}E[P(s\mid q_{i})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>c</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E[\hat{v_{s}}]=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{c}E[P(s\mid q_{i})]</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text">Since <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are chosen i.i.d, we have that</span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle E[P(s\mid q_{i})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle E[P(s\mid q_{i})]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=E[P(s\mid q_{1})]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=E[P(s\mid q_{1})].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody><tr class="ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left" style="white-space:normal;" colspan="5">Thus,</td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle E[\hat{v}_{s}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle E[\hat{v}_{s}]</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<tbody id="S3.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=E[P(s\mid q_{1})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=E[P(s\mid q_{1})]</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=E[P(s\mid p_{1})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=E[P(s\mid p_{1})]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
