</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Note that PA memorization only relies on <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, thus obviating the need for training baseline models <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m16" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="M\prime" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em">′</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\prime</annotation></semantics></math> like with counterfactual memorization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.3 </span>Target and Baseline Datasets.</h4>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_paragraph">4.1.3.1 </span>Synthetic Data</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="124" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>124</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">124</annotation></semantics></math>M parameter GPT-<math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> models with <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> Wikitext
documents in two settings, as described below. We repeat the experiments in each setting several times with different seeds and target sequences, training over <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="350" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>350</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">350</annotation></semantics></math> different models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Target Model:</span>
In this setting, we inject “near-duplicate” sequences into the dataset, a strategy commonly used to study memorization versus generalization in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
For our purposes, near-duplicates are defined as sequences sharing <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> token overlap, as illustrated in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ item 1 ‣ 4.1.3.1 Synthetic Data ‣ 4.1.3 Target and Baseline Datasets. ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
Unlike earlier studies, which often used duplicates with much higher overlap, we intentionally adopt a lower threshold to be conservative.
This choice is motivated by recent findings that removing high-overlap sequences improves model performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al. (2022)</a></cite>.
Thus, injecting highly overlapping sequences may not realistically reflect modern training regimes, where such examples are typically removed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
Our goal is to demonstrate that even with relatively low overlap, models are capable of generalizing to a given sequence without requiring many (or any) exact copies in the training data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To simulate varying degrees of generality, we vary the ratio of exact copies to near-duplicates of a target sequence injected into the training data. For example, an initial dataset may contain <math id="S4.I1.i1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="180" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>180</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">180</annotation></semantics></math> near-duplicates of a target sequence and no exact copies. In the next dataset, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math> of these near-duplicates are replaced with <math id="S4.I1.i1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> exact copies, yielding <math id="S4.I1.i1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> near-duplicates and <math id="S4.I1.i1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> exact matches. The rationale is that as more exact copies are included, the model is more likely to exhibit counterfactual memorization, predicting the target sequence because it has seen it verbatim during training. Conversely, when the dataset consists mostly of near-duplicates, the model must rely on generalization from many similar–but not identical–examples, simulating the case where a sequence is generated with high probability simply because there is a lot of similar data in the training set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite>. By carefully controlling the ratio of exact copies to near-duplicates, we can precisely modulate the extent to which the model relies on memorization versus generalization in order to reproduce the target sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We use the following number of (exact copies, near-duplicates) to create <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7</annotation></semantics></math> distinct types of datasets: <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(0,180)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0,180</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0,180)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(10,150)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10,150</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(10,150)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(20,120)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>20,120</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(20,120)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(30,90)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>90</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(30,90)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(40,60)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>60</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(40,60)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(50,30)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>30</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(50,30)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(60,0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(60,0)</annotation></semantics></math>. In every case, the total training set size remains fixed at <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> sequences, with only the composition of exact versus near-duplicate instances varying.
We repeat this process for <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> different target sequences, training <math id="S4.I1.i1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25\times 7=175" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>175</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25\times 7=175</annotation></semantics></math> different target models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">Exact Copy</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">Near-Dup</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T1.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T1.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span> <span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.2" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">Quantum doughnuts might not exist,</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">but theoretical bakers remain hopeful.</span></span>
</span></span><span id="S4.T1.2.2.1.3" class="ltx_text"></span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.1" class="ltx_text"></span> <span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">majestic<span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">um</span> Nant<span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">onuts</span> might Conradavery</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">258 texted <span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">theoretical</span> imperialistmlicks Shim.</span></span>
</span></span><span id="S4.T1.2.2.2.3" class="ltx_text"></span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>A sequence and one possible <math id="S4.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> near-duplicate. Matching tokens are highlighted</figcaption>
</figure></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Model:</span>The counterfactual memorization metric relies on a comparison between the target model and a baseline model. In accordance with the metric’s definition of a baseline model, we remove only the exact copies of the target sequence, but keep the near duplicates in the training data. So the baseline model for a target model trained with <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> near-duplicates and <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> exact copies would have only the <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> near duplicates. This is to simulate the scenario where the exact target data might be removed, but other data that can generalize to the target sequence is still present in the training dataset.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_paragraph">4.1.3.2 </span>Real Data</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we again train <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="124M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>124</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">124M</annotation></semantics></math>-parameter GPT-2 models on WikiText. Crucially, rather than manually injecting near-duplicates to simulate varying degrees of suffix commonality, we select naturally occurring
<math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> pairs from WikiText in which the suffix <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> spans a wide range of frequencies. Specifically, we focus on pairs where
<math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is a named entity, following prior work on memorization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lukas et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1.3.2 Real Data ‣ 4.1.3 Target and Baseline Datasets. ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents a frequency histogram of named entities in WikiText: for example, “United States of America” appears approximately 500 times, whereas “Starlicide” occurs only once. We sample a total of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> pairs, with <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> drawn uniformly across the frequency buckets shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1.3.2 Real Data ‣ 4.1.3 Target and Baseline Datasets. ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18733v1/ne_distribution.svg" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:384/154;" width="384" height="154"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Distribution of Named Entities across Wikitext. The x-axis shows the frequency of each Named-Entity, and the y-axis shows how many named entities fit in each bucket</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.P2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S4.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Target Model</span> In this setting, we simply train the model as-is on Wikitext without modifying the dataset.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Model</span>
In this setting, we retrain the model after removing the target sequence <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> from the WikiText training data. For example, if <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to “I live in the <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|</annotation></semantics></math> United States of America,” this exact prefix–suffix pair is excluded prior to training. Importantly, we do not remove other occurrences of the suffix <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., “United States of America”) that appear with different prefixes, since our goal is to measure memorization of the specific sequence <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> rather than the suffix in isolation.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.4 </span>Correlation Results</h4>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_paragraph">4.1.4.1 </span>Synthetic Data Results</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1.4.2 Real Data Results ‣ 4.1.4 Correlation Results ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the counterfactual memorization metric (Equation <a href="#S4.E6" title="In 4.1.2 Metric measurements. ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) on the x-axis, and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s|p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s|p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the component of PA memorization that measures the commonality of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> (Equation <a href="#S4.E7" title="In 4.1.2 Metric measurements. ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) on the y-axis. Each data point represents the average over 25 different models trained. Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1.4.2 Real Data Results ‣ 4.1.4 Correlation Results ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates that as the target sequence becomes less generic due to fewer near-duplicates, the counterfactual memorization metric (Equation (<a href="#S4.E5" title="In 4.1.1 Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>)) increases correspondingly. As hypothesized, we also observe a strong correlation between PA memorization and counterfactual memorization, suggesting that our metric indeed measures generalization from similar data. One interesting observation is the difference in the scale of the two metrics, a limitation that we discuss in more detail in Section <a href="#S4.SS8" title="4.8 Limitations ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_paragraph">4.1.4.2 </span>Real Data Results</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.4.2 Real Data Results ‣ 4.1.4 Correlation Results ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> also shows the counterfactual memorization metric (Equation <a href="#S4.E6" title="In 4.1.2 Metric measurements. ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) on the x-axis, and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s|p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s|p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math> (Equation <a href="#S4.E7" title="In 4.1.2 Metric measurements. ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) on the y-axis. Here, each of the data points represents the correlation between the PA memorization and Counterfactual memorization for each of the <math id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S4.SS1.SSS4.P2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> that we sample from WikiText. Here too, we see that both Counterfactual memorization and PA memorization tend to correlate positively.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18733v1/counterfactual-correlation.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:384/155;" width="384" height="155"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Counterfactual Memorization (x-axis) vs PA Memorization (y-axis). Each data point is an average over models with the same frequency of exact matches and near duplicates</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18733v1/wikitext-counterfactual-correlation.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:384/160;" width="384" height="160"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Counterfactual Memorization (x-axis) vs PA Memorization (y-axis). Each data point represents the scores of a single <math id="S4.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> in WikiText</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Large Scale Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Now that we’ve shown PA memorization correlates with Counterfactual Memorization, we now evaluate PA memorization by itself on large pretrained models. Since we are no longer constrained by having
We evaluate PA memorization on various sizes <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> recent generative models with open source datasets: Llama <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. (2023)</a></cite> and OPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2022)</a></cite>, which were pre-trained on the Common Crawl (Llama), or The Pile (OPT). We experiment with all available sizes of the models, namely 3B, 7B, and 13B for Llama, and 125M, 350M, 1.3B, 2.7B, 6.7B and 13B for OPT. Unless otherwise stated, the default model size for which results are displayed is OPT 6.7B and Llama 7B.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Target Sequences for Extraction</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To compute <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> for each sequence we test, we prompt the model with <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5000</annotation></semantics></math> randomly sampled sequences from their respective datasets and measure the likelihood of generating <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> in each case. We repeat this for <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> trials. Our evaluation is performed in <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> different settings:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Named Entities.</span> Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lukas et al. (2023)</a></cite>, we randomly sample <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 5000-8000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>5000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8000</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 5000-8000</annotation></semantics></math> sequences that contain Named Entities (NEs) from each of the datasets. We do this since NEs can simulate sensitive data that might be targets for extraction since they are typically names of individuals, organizations, places, etc. We must note that this is simply to emulate a realistic use-case; in reality, model developers would repeat the measurements with sequences that they consider sensitive. For consistency, each of our sequences consists of a prefix of <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> tokens followed by a <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-token long Named Entity. While we experiment with longer prefix lengths of upto <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>400</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">400</annotation></semantics></math> tokens, unless otherwise stated, the default prefix length is <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Long Sequences.</span> We also simulate extraction of longer sequences, which could be useful to measure the risk of leaking copyrighted data. For this, we randomly sample <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5000</annotation></semantics></math> sequences with <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math>-token prefixes and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math>-token suffixes from each dataset, similar to prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al. (2024)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a></cite>. Here too, we experiment with longer prefix lengths of upto <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>400</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">400</annotation></semantics></math> tokens, but unless otherwise stated, the default prefix length is <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SATML Challenge.</span> Lastly, we also perform a smaller-scale, additional analysis on the dataset in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, which consists of <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>-eidetic sequences (sequences where each <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> is known to occur only once in The Pile). This dataset was released for the 2023 SATML training data extraction challenge and consists of <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15,000</annotation></semantics></math> sequences, each with a prefix of <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> tokens followed by a suffix of <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> tokens. We present results on <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> of the <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15,000</annotation></semantics></math> sequences.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Hyper-parameters</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The only parameters that need to be tuned in Definition <a href="#Thmdefinition2" title="Definition 2 (Prior-Aware memorization). ‣ 3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> are <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒎</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{m}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">, threshold for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{P(s|p)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" lspace="0em" mathvariant="bold" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>p</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{P(s|p)}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> This parameter allows us to pick which <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> have a high risk of leakage, and thus can be adjusted based on the risk tolerance. Since <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> is a threshold for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s|p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s|p)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{m}</annotation></semantics></math> indicates, on average, the number of times a user would need to prompt the model with <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> to leak the target <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. We set <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=0.01</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-token <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=0.0001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=0.0001</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math>-token <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. We deliberately pick small values of <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> to be conservative in our estimation of memorization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{n}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">, threshold for <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" fence="true" lspace="0em" mathvariant="bold" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span> The second parameter, <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>, allows us to differentiate <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> has a large prior from those that do not. To estimate this, we compute <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> that are known to be easy-to-predict for LLMs (examples provided in <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Generic Sequences for Threshold Calculation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>). We set <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> to be the average of <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math> over these sequences. Note that since <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{\hat{v}_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a model specific quantity, the threshold is recomputed for each model tested.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Effect of Model Size on PA Memorization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Figures <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 Effect of Model Size on PA Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S4.F6.sf1" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 4.8 Limitations ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a>, we plot both the number of <em id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">extractably memorized</em> (simply high <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math>, as defined by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a></cite> and in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Generalization vs Memorization: Issues with leakage measures ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) and <em id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">PA memorized</em> sequences as a function of model size. We also plot PA memorized sequences as a proportion of the total extractably memorized sequences. There are two interesting observations to be made:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gap in extractable and PA memorized sequences</span>. Consistent with prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hayes et al. (2024)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild et al. (2024)</a></cite>, both extractable and PA memorization increase as the model size increases. However, there is a difference between number of extractably memorized and PA memorized sequences. Notably, this difference is quite large when the target suffixes are <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> token Named Entities, where as few as <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> of extractable memorized samples are PA memorized in the largest models. This suggests that most of the suffixes of extractably memorized sequences are indeed statistically popular rather than truly memorized. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.7 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, many of these <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> are indeed popular entities such as politicians, celebrities, countries, etc. More surprisingly, we note a similar result in the SATML challenge dataset in Figure <a href="#S4.F6.sf1" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 4.8 Limitations ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a>, where around <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\%</annotation></semantics></math> of sequences are “common” in nature. This is despite the fact that each sequence in the challenge dataset occurs only once in the entire training data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decreasing proportion of PA memorized sequences.</span> Secondly, Figures <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 Effect of Model Size on PA Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S4.F6.sf1" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 4.8 Limitations ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a> show that as model size increases, the proportion of PA memorized sequences generally <em id="S4.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decreases</em>. This suggests that larger models are increasingly able to reproduce verbatim text by generalizing from common or near-duplicate data, rather than through true memorization—a finding consistent with recent work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18733v1/counterfactual-size.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="width:38.586em; height:10.220em;aspect-ratio:513/117;" width="513" height="117"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>The primary y-axis reports the number of extractable and PA memorized sequences as a function of model size for 4- and 50-token suffixes. The thicker lines denote the proportion of extractable-memorized sequences that are also PA memorized, with their scale indicated on the secondary y-axis.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Effect of Prefix Length on Discovering PA Memorization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.6 Effect of Prefix Length on Discovering PA Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> we plot the number of samples labeled as PA memorized and extractable memorized as a function of the length of prompt <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> provided to the model. Unsurprisingly, we observe that longer <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>’s can discover more PA memorized sequences. However, note that the PA memorized of <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> token Named Entity suffixes does not benefit as much from longer prefixes as the <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> token suffixes. Again, this is likely due to the fact that many of these Named Entities (<em id="S4.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.,</em>United States of America) are popular occurrences in web-text, and likely do not need specific prompts to be produced correctly.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18733v1/counterfactual-len.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="width:40.633em; height:9.179em;aspect-ratio:540/105;" width="540" height="105"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Number of a) Extractable, and b) PA Memorized Sequences as a function of model prefix length for two types of suffixes.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.7 </span>Qualitative Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.7 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows a few sequences with 4-token Named Entity suffixes that have high and low PA memorization scores (i.e., <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}</annotation></semantics></math>). We present more such examples in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C PA Memorization Examples ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. We note that all of the sequences with low scores have suffixes that are places, political figures, etc. We also attempt to verify how “rare” the high-scoring sequences are. While it is infeasible to determine rarity precisely within a dataset with trillions of tokens, we perform a web-search and note that the high-scoring sequences have very few search results. In fact, the highest scoring sequence in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.7 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> has just a single search result, which is precisely the sequence that is included in the dataset. We also note that high-scoring suffixes do appear to be more “artifact-like” than their low-scoring counterparts, which appear to be more natural text. This is more apparent in longer sequences, such as the examples presented in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C PA Memorization Examples ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.8 </span>Limitations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One limitation of PA memorization compared to counterfactual memorization is that <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s;M)</annotation></semantics></math> can be large due to either many near-duplicates <em id="S4.SS8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">or</em> even due to many exact copies of <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math>. This is illustrated in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>, where we attempt to reduce the statistical likelihood of <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> by replacing near-duplicates with fewer exact copies. However, as shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F6.sf2" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 4.8 Limitations ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(b)</span></a>, both <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s;M)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p;M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p;M)</annotation></semantics></math> increase when exact copies are added, even though near-duplicates are removed to lower the commonality of <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. As a result, <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p;M)}{P(s)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p;M)}{P(s)}</annotation></semantics></math> increases very <em id="S4.SS8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">slowly</em> as more exact copies are added (y-axis in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1.4.2 Real Data Results ‣ 4.1.4 Correlation Results ‣ 4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), indicating our metric may be less effective than counterfactual memorization at distinguishing whether a high <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> arises from near-duplicates or from exact copies.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F6.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18733v1/counterfactual-breakdown.svg" id="S4.F6.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/277;" width="548" height="277"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span><math id="S4.F6.sf2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F6.sf2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the number of exact copies of <math id="S4.F6.sf2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> in the training dataset.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Results on the SATML Challenge Dataset (a), and <math id="S4.F6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> from Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Correlation with Counterfactual Memorization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2019)</a></cite> was one of the first works to examine memorization in LLMs, and did so by introducing canaries during training and measuring their perplexity compared to random data during inference. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2021)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. (2022)</a></cite> measured leakage of training data and examined memorization scaling laws in LLMs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite> provide new methods to be able to increase leakage of training data from LLMs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hayes et al. (2024)</a></cite> explores probabilistic metrics for quantifying memorization. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lukas et al. (2023)</a></cite> study leakage of PII in LLMs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kassem et al. (2024)</a></cite> leverage one LLM for prompt-optimization to leak data from another LLM. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al. (2024)</a></cite> attempt to predict which sequences will be memorized by an LLM using lower-compute trial runs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduce the notion of sequence-likelihood, the metric that we use for our analysis. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tirumala et al. (2022)</a></cite> explore scaling laws and examine memorization dynamics throughout training. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al. (2024)</a></cite> study scaling laws for “fact memorization” within LLMs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2022)</a></cite> study trends in both memorization, and <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">association</em> of PII, where the latter involves leakage through prompts that are not verbatim training sequences.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feldman (2020)</a></cite> introduces the idea of the “long-tail”, where they show that models have a tendency to memorize rare, out-of-distribution samples. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maini et al. (2023)</a></cite> explore whether memorization can be localized to certain parts of the model. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ippolito et al. (2023)</a></cite> argue that focusing solely on verbatim memorization provides an incomplete picture of privacy risks. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartmann et al. (2023)</a></cite> provides a systematic overview of the work done in the memorization space. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Morris et al. (2025)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild et al. (2024)</a></cite> use compression-based techniques in order to estimate if sequences are memorized. In particular <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Morris et al. (2025)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. (2024)</a></cite> aim to also disentangle memorization from generalization, however, their method relies on having a model that embodies the true distribution of data, and it is unclear if this is practical in the large-scale settings we see today.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we propose a novel method to identify whether a sequence is counterfactually memorized without having to train different baseline models. Our method shows that at worst <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of sequences labeled as memorized by prior metrics, are in fact, statistically likely sequences that could be produced without specifically training on the exact sequences. This highlights how traditional metrics may overstate memorization in LLMs by labeling generic sequences as memorized.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="bib" class="ltx_bibliography">

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Proof for Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 3.2 𝑃(𝑠,𝑀): generality of 𝑠 ‣ 3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a></h2>

<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_paragraph">A.0.0.1 </span>Theorem <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Var[\hat{v_{s}}]=\frac{1}{c}\cdot Var[P(s\mid p_{i})]\leq\frac{1}{4c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>c</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Var[\hat{v_{s}}]=\frac{1}{c}\cdot Var[P(s\mid p_{i})]\leq\frac{1}{4c}</annotation></semantics></math></p>

<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">As in Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3.2 𝑃(𝑠,𝑀): generality of 𝑠 ‣ 3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the transition from conditioning on <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.P1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> follows from the equality of their distributions.
∎</span></p>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Generic Sequences for Threshold Calculation</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide a list of some short and long simple sequences that we use to calculate the threshold <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> in Definition <a href="#Thmdefinition2" title="Definition 2 (Prior-Aware memorization). ‣ 3 Our Metric: Prior-Aware (PA) Memorization ‣ Prior Aware Memorization: An Efficient Metric for Distinguishing Memorization from Generalization in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The short sequences are used to calculate the threshold for the short, <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-token suffixes, while the long sequences are used to calculate the threshold for the longer <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math>-token suffixes. In each case, each sequence is divided into equal tokens of prefix and suffix used to calculate <math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}</annotation></semantics></math>. Recall that <math id="A2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is simply an average of <math id="A2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">

<li id="A2.I1.i11" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i11.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.I1.i11.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this article, we will discuss the basics of this topic and explain why it is important to understand this concept in the broader context of the field. We will begin with a brief introduction, followed by a step-by-step explanation of the main ideas, and finally provide some examples to illustrate how these principles can be applied in practice. Whether you are completely new to this topic or simply looking for a refresher, this guide is designed to help you gain a clear and practical understanding.,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i12" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i12.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i12.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The purpose of this guide is to help you get started with the software in a straightforward and beginner-friendly way. First, we will walk through the installation process and highlight common issues that may arise during setup. Then we will cover the essential features you need to know to be productive right away. By the end of this guide, you should have a working environment and a solid foundation that will allow you to explore more advanced aspects of the software at your own pace.,</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>PA Memorization Examples</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide examples of <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\|s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\|s</annotation></semantics></math> that have statistically likely <math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and those that do not. Each sequence is preceded by it’s value of <math id="A3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{P(s\mid p)}{P(s)}</annotation></semantics></math>, presented in colored text. The suffix <math id="A3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is presented in bold text. We note that low-scoring sequences have more natural-appearing english text, which is common in the training data for both OPT and Llama models. However, high-scoring sequences tend to have excessive formatting, non-english characters, URLs, are about niche topics, or are boiler-plate text (e.g., terms and conditions from companies) that appear verbatim several times on the web.</p>
</div>

              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
